# Detecting and controlling microbes

> *This chapter closes Part I with the practical questions: how do we find out which microbe is
> present, and how do we get rid of microbes we do not want? Both answers follow from the traits
> in the earlier chapters.*

## Every method reads something {#sec-det-reads}

A laboratory method never shows you "the organism". It reads one property, and what it reads sets
what it can and cannot tell you. Keeping that in mind explains most of what seems arbitrary about
diagnostic microbiology.

<div data-island="sorter" data-src="/diagrams/method-sorter.yml"></div>

## Seeing: stains and microscopy {#sec-det-microscopy}

Microscopy is fast, cheap and available everywhere, and it reads structure. You met the Gram stain in
the *How bacteria are built and get energy* chapter: it reads the envelope, sorting most bacteria into
two groups within minutes. The acid-fast stain reads a waxy, mycolic-acid wall, which is why it finds
mycobacteria that the Gram stain misses.

The limits follow from what a stain reads. It gives a category, not a species: purple cocci in chains
could be several organisms. It needs enough organisms to be present, typically around 10⁴ to 10⁵ per
millilitre of fluid, so a negative result does not exclude infection. And organisms with no wall, or
too thin to resolve, give nothing useful.

## Growing: culture {#sec-det-culture}

Culture reads growth. Its advantage over every other method is that it yields a **living isolate**,
which can then be identified, tested against drugs, and compared with isolates from other patients in
an outbreak investigation.

Media are chosen for what they allow or reveal:

| Type of medium | What it does | Example of use |
|---|---|---|
| **Non-selective** | Supports a wide range of organisms | A general plate for a normally sterile sample |
| **Enriched** | Adds nutrients that fastidious organisms cannot make | Chocolate agar, which supplies factors released from lysed red cells |
| **Selective** | Contains agents that suppress unwanted organisms | Isolating one pathogen from a sample full of normal microbiota |
| **Differential** | Makes colonies look different according to a metabolic property | Blood agar, where haemolysis distinguishes streptococci |

Culture conditions decide what a laboratory can find. An anaerobe will not grow on a plate left in
air, as in the lab case in the *How bacteria are built and get energy* chapter. A slow-growing
organism will be missed by a laboratory that discards plates too early, as in the Helicobacter case.
An obligate intracellular organism will not grow on agar at all. None of these failures means the
sample contained nothing.

Culture is also slow. Many bacteria need overnight incubation, and mycobacteria can take weeks. That
delay is the main reason molecular methods have become central.

## Detecting molecules {#sec-det-molecular}

**Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs)**, of which the polymerase chain reaction is the familiar
example, copy a target sequence many times until it can be detected. They are fast, extremely
sensitive, and can find organisms that cannot be cultured.

Three consequences of what they read are worth knowing:

- They detect *sequence, not life*. A positive result can come from dead organisms or residual
  nucleic acid after an infection has resolved, so a positive test does not always mean a current,
  active infection.
- They find *only what they look for*. A test designed for one organism will not report another,
  unlike culture, which can grow the unexpected.
- Their sensitivity makes **contamination** a real problem, which is why laboratories separate
  pre- and post-amplification work.

**MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry** reads the protein profile of a colony and matches it against a
database, identifying most organisms in minutes once they have grown. It has largely replaced long
sequences of biochemical tests. **Whole-genome sequencing** reads the entire genome, at a resolution
that can establish whether two patients' isolates are the same strain, which is now standard in
outbreak investigation.

## Reading the host: serology {#sec-det-serology}

Serology detects the patient's **antibodies**, so it is evidence about the host's experience rather
than about the organism's current presence. Two patterns carry most of the interpretation. IgM
appears early and falls; IgG appears later and persists, sometimes for life. A **rise in antibody
level between paired samples** taken one to two weeks apart indicates recent infection.

The usual pitfall follows directly: a single positive IgG result may reflect an infection years ago,
or vaccination. Serology is most useful for organisms that are hard to culture, for infections
diagnosed after the organism has gone, and for assessing immunity.

## Testing drug susceptibility {#sec-det-mic}

Once an organism has been grown, its susceptibility can be measured. The standard quantity is the
**minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC)**: the lowest concentration of a drug that prevents visible
growth.

<div data-island="mic-reader" data-src="/diagrams/mic-reader.yml"></div>

The laboratory converts the MIC into a category using a **breakpoint**, the concentration agreed to
separate organisms likely to respond from those that are not. Breakpoints come from committees such
as EUCAST and CLSI and are revised as evidence accumulates, so they are looked up rather than
memorised. Two cautions matter at this stage. A report of "susceptible" describes the organism in a
tube, not the patient: the drug still has to reach the site of infection at an adequate
concentration. And a result is only as good as the sample, which is why samples are ideally taken
before treatment starts.

## Controlling microbes {#sec-det-control}

Three terms are used precisely in practice and loosely in conversation. **Sterilisation** kills or
removes all microbial life, including bacterial spores. **Disinfection** removes most organisms from
an inanimate object, but not reliably spores. **Antisepsis** is the same idea applied to living
tissue, such as skin preparation before a procedure.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-sterilisation-disinfection.yml"></div>

Methods differ in what survives them, and the survivors are predictable from earlier chapters.
Bacterial spores survive boiling and alcohol, so instruments entering sterile tissue are autoclaved.
Enveloped viruses are easily inactivated by alcohol and detergents, because their lipid envelope is
fragile, while naked viruses are more resistant, which is why hand washing matters in outbreaks of
hand, foot and mouth disease. Prions resist routine sterilisation entirely and need specific extended
protocols.

For hands, the practical rule follows the same logic. An alcohol rub is faster and more effective for
most organisms, but when spores are a concern, soap and water are preferred, because washing removes
physically what alcohol does not kill.

## Preventing infection {#sec-det-prevent}

Prevention works at the links of the chain in the previous chapter. Two deserve naming here.

**Vaccination** makes a host immune without disease. Vaccines contain inactivated organisms, live
attenuated organisms, purified components such as proteins or capsular polysaccharides, **toxoids**
(inactivated protein toxins), or nucleic acid encoding an antigen. Two principles recur. Capsular
polysaccharides alone produce a poor response in young children, so they are **conjugated** to a
protein, which is why conjugate vaccines transformed protection against encapsulated organisms. And
vaccination protects the unvaccinated too, by reducing transmission, which is the herd immunity
effect from the previous chapter. The immunology block covers the mechanisms.

**Antimicrobial stewardship** reduces selection for resistance by using antimicrobials only when
indicated, at the right dose and duration. The *How bacteria copy themselves and change* chapter
explains why this is a population-level problem rather than an individual one.

## Where Part I has got to {#sec-det-close}

You now have the toolkit the rest of the book uses: how microbes are built, how they get energy, how
they change, how they cause damage, how they spread, and how they are found and controlled. Part II
takes each group of organisms in turn and asks the same six questions of it. The answers differ; the
questions do not.
